messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: negative binomial mystery solved
parts:
Figured it out. It's a numerical problem. The negative binomial log-pdf is

lgamma(alpha+x) - lgamma(alpha)
+ alpha * log(beta) - (alpha + x) * log(beta + 1)
- lgamma(x+1).

When alpha and beta are O(1e16), effectively alpha+x=alpha and
beta+1=beta. Then the first two lines disappear, and the result
becomes independent of alpha and beta. I'm rewriting
neg_binomial_log() and binomial_coefficient_log() to be more
numerically stable using Stirling's approximation

lgamma(x+1) = x*log(x) - x + 0.5*log(2*pi*x) + 1/(12*x) ...

and the identity

a*log(alpha+x) - b*log(alpha)
= a*log(alpha+x) - b*log(alpha+x) - b*log(alpha/(alpha+x))
= (a - b) * log(alpha+x) - b*log(alpha/(alpha+x))

I'll let you know when it's pushed.

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] negative binomial mystery solved
parts:
It turns out I spoke too soon. There's a statistical issue in addition
to the numerical issue.

We're using the gamma-mixture parameterization, which says that
y ~ neg_binomial(α, β)
is equivalent to
z ~ gamma(α, β)
y ~ Poisson(z).
Suppose α=1e1000 and β=2e1000. Then this model basically reduces to
y ~ Poisson(1/2),
since the std deviation of z is 0.5e-500. (I think that's
right--anyway, it's basically 0.)

The problem is that when you put a uniform prior on alpha and beta you
wind up with an improper posterior, since you can make alpha and beta
as large as you want and still have the data be within the realm of
plausibility as long as the ratio alpha/beta doesn't get crazy.

So this isn't a valid model--you absolutely, positively need a prior.
On the plus side, I know a lot more about the negative binomial than I
used to!

I'll push the changes regardless, along with a cutoff that turns the
negative-binomial into the equivalent Poisson when alpha/beta^2 gets
small enough.

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] negative binomial mystery solved
parts:
> Given our previous problem with gamma mixtures in the Cauchy,
> I was wondering if that would be a problem.

I think this is a pretty different kind of problem than slow sampling
for the Cauchy. There, we're just up against the standard
computational challenges of MCMC with heavy-tailed distributions.
Here, we're up against the (impossible) challenge of sampling from an
improper distribution.

This issue brings up sort of an interesting question for these sorts
of heavy-tailed distributions in general. For example, what's an
appropriate non-informative prior on the number of degrees of freedom
of a t? Clearly not uniform(0,∞), since that's going to run into
exactly the same problem. The crux of the issue is that, for any
positive c, under that improper prior
p(degrees of freedom > c) = 1
p(data | degrees of freedom > c) > 0
so
p(degrees of freedom > c | data) = 1.

So what's a non-informative prior for that degrees-of-freedom
parameter? What's a weakly informative prior?

Matt

of heavy-tailed distributions in general. For example, what's an
appropriate non-informative prior on the number of degrees of freedom
of a t? Clearly not uniform(0,∞), since that's going to run into
exactly the same problem. The crux of the issue is that, for any
positive c, under that improper prior
p(degrees of freedom > c) = 1
p(data | degrees of freedom > c) > 0
so
p(degrees of freedom > c | data) = 1.

So what's a non-informative prior for that degrees-of-freedom
parameter? What's a weakly informative prior?

If you had a belief about the mean degrees of freedom, then the maximum entropy distribution in this case is exponential.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_entropy_probability_distribution#Positive_and_given_mean:_the_exponential_distribution

Without a belief about the mean, I don't think there is a maximum entropy distribution in this case.

Ben

The point is that I want to weasel out of expressing a prior belief
about the mean!

But the point is also that that's clearly not an option, since in this
case a uniform prior on the default parameterization actually
corresponds to quite a strong prior belief.

Matt
